# Local CI configuration

The workflow runs on push or manual dispatch. It uses standard Windows and Apple Silicon macOS runners, a read-only repository token, and commit-pinned actions. It creates test artifacts, an unsigned per-user Windows installer, an Android APK and an ad-hoc signed Mac DMG. It does not publish releases, deploy a service, or require signing secrets.

The browser checks use the runner's existing Edge/Chrome and synthetic camera/audio sources. They prove protocol and local media behavior, not physical Android/Mac operation or internet reachability. Android bridge unit tests exercise the native-call contract and transport lifecycle.

The Android job uses Java 21, SDK platform 36 and build tools 36.0.0. It calls the manual `scripts/build-android.ps1` compiler and APK verifier, then executes the production pinned-Java transport security fixture. It creates a temporary development signing key on the isolated runner; the key is never uploaded. Each CI build can use a different development key, so these APK artifacts are testing builds and may require uninstalling an earlier differently signed test APK. Published release APKs are built locally with the retained private key, so they preserve update continuity with the earlier local release.

The Mac job uses `macos-15`, which is a standard arm64 runner. Standard public-repository jobs are free under [GitHub's hosted-runner terms](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners). The job checks the actual runner architecture, compiles the Swift input helper for `arm64-apple-macos13.0`, runs nine safe checks without posting input, and builds an Apple Silicon DMG. It then mounts the actual DMG read-only and verifies its integrity, app/helper architecture, usage descriptions, deep code signature, bundled source hashes, actual Electron renderer launch, and pinned local HTTPS room start/stop. The evidence distinguishes this build check from physical Mac camera, microphone, screen recording and remote-input testing.

Mac testing builds use explicit ad-hoc signing (`mac.identity: "-"`) and retain hardened runtime. The [electron-builder v26 signing guide](https://www.electron.build/v26/docs/features/code-signing/code-signing-mac/) explains why ad-hoc Electron builds need library-validation exceptions. The minimal entitlements file includes JIT and library validation exceptions plus camera/audio input entitlements. These builds have no paid Developer ID certificate or Apple notarization, so the Mac owner must approve opening the test app through macOS Privacy & Security. Camera/microphone prompts appear only on an explicit local capture action; screen recording and Accessibility remain separate owner permissions. [Electron's permission APIs](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/system-preferences) are used for actual status and sensor requests, and [Apple's Accessibility trust check](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/applicationservices/1459186-axisprocesstrustedwithoptions) is enforced by the input helper. The app includes a Local Network usage description and must receive the owner's separate LAN permission on macOS 15+. [Apple TN3179](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3179-understanding-local-network-privacy) explains that ad-hoc signatures can make LAN permission identity less reliable across builds; the free testing build is not a substitute for a Developer ID release. New [Electron local-network permission types](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/session) are allowed only for the bundled main frame after the main process prepares a pinned invitation or a local room.

Only top-level JSON/PNG evidence and installer outputs are uploaded. SDKs, signing keys, certificate fixtures and dependency folders are excluded. Confirm the corresponding remote Actions run and artifact evidence for each release. The separate manually dispatched Android runtime workflow installs an exact APK artifact into an isolated API36 emulator, then checks owner consent, native projection frames and attended Accessibility input. It targets emulator serials and the named AuralinkAPI36 AVD only. Physical microphone, speaker and vendor-specific behavior remain real-device checks.
